Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Draw as the engineer who has to live with the decision, not as a decorator: a diagram earns its place when it lets a cold reader see a mechanism they would otherwise have to assemble from prose — where data flows, which components talk, what changes between two options, what state a request moves through. If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on — the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves — and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes — the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on — no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` — no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end — never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11–13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool — simplify instead.

## How the human actually stays in the loop

It's not a single "approve at the end" checkpoint — it's enforced at the data-model level in a few concrete ways:

1. **Nothing is authoritative until it's `tracked`.** Every AI output — findings, clusters, draft requirements, scores — lives in states (`draft`, `proposed`) that are explicitly non-final. The agents can run the entire pipeline unattended and produce a full candidate backlog, but none of it counts as "BMW's requirements" until a PM moves it across a gate.
2. **The PM has exactly four verbs, and each is a distinct, logged transition**: *Approve* (→ tracked), *Reject* (terminal, but kept visible, not deleted), *Edit* (PM rewrites the content directly — the diff is the audit event), *Challenge* (PM attaches a note like "evidence too thin for US" — this becomes a scoped instruction back to a specific agent, not a vague "try again").
3. **The UI won't let a status change commit without a rationale string.** That's what makes the audit trail "documented rationale" rather than just a timestamp.
4. **There are two separate gates before anything is fully official** (Fig. 1/4 in the doc): content gate (is this requirement even right?) and priority gate (is this score right?) — so a PM isn't rubber-stamping one bundled decision.
5. **PM can override two different things independently**: the *scoring weights* (re-run Prioritization Agent with new weights) and the *evidence trust* on a specific finding (e.g. downgrade a shaky competitor review to "Weak" — this recomputes the score and is logged).
6. **Standing requirements don't drift silently.** The Delta Check only ever *proposes* re-review; it never updates a tracked requirement's status on its own.

## Tracing "what features do we need to stay competitive in the US?"

This is a different entry point into the same agent graph, not a new pipeline. Here's what actually happens:

1. **PM asks the question in a chat/query box**, scoped (explicitly or by current UI context) to `vehicle_line` + `market=US`.
2. **Orchestrator checks the knowledge base first** — are there already findings/clusters tagged `market:US` for this vehicle line from the standing pipeline? Say it finds 14.
3. **If coverage looks thin, it dispatches targeted agents on demand**: Market & Competitor Agent runs a fresh scoped web search ("US midsize sedan segment, competitor features, 2026–2030"), Customer Feedback Agent re-filters the existing feedback/customer-study files down to US respondents only. Say that adds 9 more findings.
4. **Requirements Drafting + Prioritization Agents run on that combined set**, same logic as the batch pipeline, and produce a ranked candidate list — each item with its linked findings, an evidence level, and *why it's US-specific* (e.g. "3 of 4 corroborating findings are US-only; EU evidence doesn't support this").

Nothing from an ad-hoc question skips the gate just because a PM asked for it.
6. **The question itself is an audit event** — query text, timestamp, PM identity, and what evidence set it drew on — so "why did we start looking at this" is traceable even for exploratory asks, not just the formal backlog.

So the answer the PM sees isn't "here's what you must build" — it's "here's a cited, confidence-graded shortlist, here's which parts rest on thin or US-only evidence, approve what holds up." The system proposes; it never promotes itself.

# Agents

> Status: `draft` · Last updated: 2026-10-10

Every agent reads some slice of evidence and produces either new evidence (`Finding`s) or a
synthesis of existing evidence (`Cluster`, `Requirement`, `Score`, dossier). None of them change a
requirement's status, priority tier, or scope on their own — see
[`02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md`](02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md) for how
their output actually gets used.

## Roster

| Agent | Stage | Reads | Produces |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline Agent | 01 Situation analysis | Previous-gen feedback, BMW portfolio docs, prior sales trend | Findings tagged `strategic_continuity` |
| Customer Feedback Agent | 01 | `*_feedback_hackathon.xlsx`, `*_customer_studies.xlsx` | Findings (`complaint` / `unmet_need` / `praise`), each with sample size + market |
| Sales & Portfolio Agent | 01 | `sales_volumes.xlsx`, parsed OptionList rows | Revealed-preference findings — option uptake % as a `business_signal` input |
| Competitor Agent | 01 | Live web search — competitor spec pages, reviews, teardown data | Findings tagged `competitor_advantage`, source-trust tier |
| Market & Trend Agent | 01 | Live web search — trend reports, forward-looking analyst pieces | Findings tagged `market_trend`; explicitly flagged as assumption-heavy, not fact |
| Clustering / Ontology Agent | 02 | All findings across sources | Deduplicated clusters mapped onto the domain taxonomy |
| Critic Agent | cross-cutting | Any agent's draft output before it reaches the PM | Verifies every claim has a live citation; flags unsupported or weakly-sourced statements and forces a retry before the step reaches `awaiting_review` |
| Requirements Drafting Agent (Synthesizer) | 03 | Clusters + linked findings | Draft requirement: description, metric, acceptance criteria |
| Prioritization Agent | 04 | Draft requirements + findings + sales/option data | Score + weight breakdown + one-line rationale |
| Documentation Agent | 05 | Every accepted step + every PM decision in a run | Human-readable dossier (markdown), re-embedded into the knowledge layer |
| Delta / Tracking Agent | ongoing | New ingestion batches vs. existing requirement evidence | `new evidence` / `contradicting` / `stale` flags, routed to PM review |

Competitor and Market/Trend are kept as **two separate agents**, not one: competitor findings are
closer to verifiable fact (a rival ships a feature or doesn't), while trend findings are inherently
speculative (what will 2030 customers want). Collapsing them into one "market research" agent was
the original shape of this design — splitting them keeps that evidence-character difference
visible in each requirement's assumptions. See
[`decisions/0003-critic-agent-and-agent-split.md`](../decisions/0003-critic-agent-and-agent-split.md).

## The Critic Agent

The Critic doesn't sit at a stage of its own — it sits between every agent and the PM. Before any
step reaches `awaiting_review`, the Critic Agent:

1. Checks that every factual claim in the agent's output links to a real source with a locator
   (page/row for provided files, URL + retrieval date for web sources).
2. Flags claims that don't — the step is automatically sent back for a retry (same agent, same
   scope, instructed to either find a citation or drop the claim) *before* the PM ever sees it.
3. Downgrades `evidence_level` on anything that's technically cited but thin (single source, no
   corroboration, low source-trust tier) rather than silently passing it through at full confidence.

This is what makes "push back on agent results" cheap for the PM: obviously weak output never
reaches the review queue in the first place. The PM still pushes back on anything the Critic let
through but the PM disagrees with — that's a normal `Retry` or `Reject` action on the step, see
next doc.

## Orchestrator

Not an agent that produces findings — the thing that holds the `PipelineRun`/`Step` state machine
(see next doc), decides which steps are unlocked, and routes a PM's "run this agent" click to the
right agent with the right scope and the right accumulated context from prior accepted steps.

# Prioritization

> Status: `draft` · Last updated: 2026-10-10

A composite score the PM can see decomposed, re-weight, and override — never a black-box rank. It
balances what BMW's own slide calls "Customer" against "Business," plus the brief's allowance for
a rough cost/effort factor.

```
score = w_c · customer_relevance + w_b · business_signal + w_s · strategic_fit − w_e · effort_proxy
```

Default weights (PM-editable per program): `w_c = 0.40`, `w_b = 0.25`, `w_s = 0.15`, `w_e = 0.20`.
Not tuned to any real dataset — a defensible starting point, nothing more.

| Component | Derived from |
|---|---|
| `customer_relevance` | Finding prevalence normalized by sample size, sentiment severity, cross-source corroboration count, market-weighted when several markets are in scope |
| `business_signal` | Uptake % of the related option in `sales_volumes.xlsx`, plus competitor-coverage gap from the Competitor Agent. A sellability proxy, not a cost model — pricing/business-case math is out of scope |
| `strategic_fit` | Continuity with the previous-generation baseline (Baseline Agent) and the PM's stated themes for this program |
| `effort_proxy` | Coarse Low/Med/High heuristic (new hardware > software/UX change). Deliberately rough, always PM-editable |
| `confidence` | Evidence-level mix + source independence count. Shown as a **separate badge**, never folded silently into rank, so "high potential, thin evidence" stays visually distinct from "confidently low priority" |

Every stored `Score` keeps the weight vector used, each raw component value, who/what computed it,
a timestamp, and a one-line generated rationale — see
[`04-data-model.md`](04-data-model.md#score) — and is versioned, so re-scoring after new evidence
never erases what a priority call used to look like.

## Worked example

`R-2031` — *Fast-response seat ventilation*, built around BMW's own slide example.

- **Score:** 0.49 / 1.00 → Tier 2 (should-have). Tiers: ≥0.65 must-have, 0.40–0.65 should-have,
  <0.40 watch-list.
- **customer_relevance 0.78** — two independent BMW-internal findings (a verbatim complaint and a
  customer-study item scored 2.9/5, n=340, EU) corroborate a comfort gap.
- **business_signal 0.41** — moderate option-uptake signal; one competitor review notes a faster
  rival response time (review-estimated, not lab-verified — flagged as an assumption).
- **strategic_fit 0.60** — aligns with the program's stated comfort-parity theme.
- **effort_proxy low** — software/calibration change, not new hardware.
- **confidence 0.65** — moderate; EU-only sample so far, no lab-verified benchmark yet.

Rationale (agent-generated): *"Two independent BMW-internal sources plus one competitor review
corroborate a comfort gap; moderate business signal from option uptake; low estimated effort —
lands mid-tier pending a lab-verified response-time benchmark."*

Full linked findings, assumptions, and its audit trail are in
[`07-audit-trail.md`](07-audit-trail.md#worked-example-r-2031).

This is the *long-horizon* state of a requirement once it has made it out of a
[run](02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md) — weeks to months, across the life of the
~two-year requirements program, not the minutes-scale step-by-step approval inside a single run.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft
    Draft --> PM_Review: PM reviews
    PM_Review --> Tracked: approve
    PM_Review --> Rejected: reject
    PM_Review --> Challenged: challenge / request evidence
    Challenged --> Draft: agent re-research
    Tracked --> Delta_Check: scheduled re-ingestion
    Delta_Check --> Tracked: no material change
    Delta_Check --> PM_Review: new / contradicting evidence
    Tracked --> Superseded: PM supersedes
    Rejected --> [*]
    Superseded --> [*]
```

- **`Draft` and `Delta_Check` run unattended.** Every other transition needs a PM action and a
  recorded reason — same four verbs as everywhere else in this system: approve, reject, edit
  (not shown as a separate state — it mutates `Draft` in place), challenge.
- **"No material change" stays quiet.** The Delta Agent re-checks tracked requirements against
  freshly ingested evidence on a recurring schedule (~quarterly) and only re-opens `PM_Review` when
  something actually moved — new corroboration, a contradiction, or evidence old enough to flag as
  stale. It never updates a tracked requirement's status on its own.
- **This is the "requirements tracking" loop** from BMW's own process slide, and the mechanism
  behind "the requirement process isn't performed once — it's a process over ~2 years."

## Relationship to the per-run approval chain

A requirement enters this state machine at `Draft` the moment a
[`PipelineRun`](02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md#data-model-additions)'s Documentation
step is accepted. Everything before that — launching each agent, reviewing its human-readable
output, retrying or rejecting a step — happens *inside* the run, at a finer grain than this
diagram shows. Think of this doc as "what happens after the research is done and a requirement
exists," and [`02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md`](02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md)
as "how the research itself gets approved."

## Committee / board mode

For the "large committee discusses this" pattern: several `Tracked`-or-`PM_Review` requirements
can be bundled into a generated board pack (a set of Documentation Agent dossiers). The
committee's collective call is still recorded as **one** audit event, with participants and
rationale noted, against one accountable PM — diffusing the discussion is fine, diffusing
accountability for the recorded decision is not.

# 0001 — Two-tier PDF ingestion instead of naive text extraction

> Date: 2026-10-10 · Status: accepted

## Context

The provided PDFs (`*_OptionList.PDF`) are structured option/equipment listings. The brief asks
for findings and requirements that are traceable to their sources. A naive "dump the PDF to text,
chunk by token count, embed" pipeline would destroy the table structure and produce citations like
"chunk 47" instead of a page/row a PM could actually go look at.

## Decision

Parse every PDF (and, by extension, every source) on two tracks:

1. **Deterministic** — layout-aware table extraction into typed rows, no model in the loop. Feeds
   structured stores (e.g. an `Options` table) directly.
2. **Semantic** — heading-aware chunking + embedding for narrative text, locator kept per chunk.

Both converge on a `Finding` with a locator and an `evidence_level` set by *how* it was extracted
(`Verified` for deterministic, `Interpreted` for semantic — further gradable by the Critic Agent
or a PM override).

## Consequences

- More ingestion code than a single embed-everything pipeline.
- Every citation in the UI can point at an exact row or page, not an approximate chunk.
- `evidence_level` becomes a meaningful, inspectable field instead of a constant.

See [`../architecture/03-ingestion.md`](../architecture/03-ingestion.md).

# 0003 — Add a Critic Agent; split Competitor from Market/Trend

> Date: 2026-10-10 · Status: accepted

## Context

Original agent roster had one "Market & Competitor Agent" and relied entirely on `evidence_level`
grading plus the PM's own judgment to catch weak or unsupported claims. A reference architecture
sketch (layered component view, not authored in this repo) proposed two changes worth adopting.

## Decision

1. **Add a Critic Agent** that sits between every agent and the PM review queue: verifies every
   claim has a live citation, forces a retry on anything unsupported, and downgrades
   `evidence_level` on thin-but-technically-cited claims — *before* the PM ever sees the output.
2. **Split Competitor from Market/Trend** into two agents. Competitor findings are close to
   verifiable fact (a rival ships a feature or it doesn't); market/trend findings are inherently
   speculative (what will 2030 customers want). Keeping them separate keeps that evidence-character
   difference visible on each requirement's assumptions, instead of averaging it away inside one
   "market research" blob.

## Consequences

- One more agent in the roster, but it directly cheapens "push back on agent results" for the PM —
  obviously weak output is caught before it reaches a human.
- Assumptions/uncertainties on a requirement can now distinguish "this rests on a competitor fact"
  from "this rests on a trend guess."

See [`../architecture/01-agents.md`](../architecture/01-agents.md).

# Orchestration & human-in-the-loop: run one agent at a time, on purpose > Status: `draft` · Last updated: 2026-10-10 This is the central mechanic of the whole system. Earlier drafts of this architecture gated the PM in at two points — after a requirement was drafted, and after it was scored. That's not tight enough: it lets four research agents run unattended, hand their combined output to a synthesizer, and only then ask the PM "does this look right?" — by which point pushing back on one bad finding means re-doing all of it. Instead: **the pipeline doesn't advance to the next agent until the PM has explicitly launched and accepted the current one.** Every agent run is a reviewable, retryable, rejectable unit on its own. ## The unit of work: a Step A `PipelineRun` (one end-to-end execution, scoped to a vehicle line + market + trigger) is made of `Step`s, one per agent invocation. A step only has five states: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> queued queued --> awaiting_launch: dependencies accepted, unlocked awaiting_launch --> running: PM clicks "Run" running --> awaiting_review: agent finishes,
Critic Agent has verified citations,
human-readable summary attached awaiting_review --> accepted: PM Accept awaiting_review --> running: PM Retry (with a steering note) awaiting_review --> rejected: PM Reject accepted --> [*]: unlocks dependent step(s) rejected --> [*]: PM decides skip-this-agent or abort run ``` Two things are deliberate: - **`awaiting_launch` is a real, separate state from `running`.** Accepting step N does not auto-start step N+1 — it only *unlocks* it. The PM still clicks "Run." This is what "click to each agent step by step before it is run" means literally: the PM is the one who starts every agent, not just the one who reviews what already ran. - **The Critic Agent sits inside `running → awaiting_review`**, not after it. A step doesn't reach the PM until every claim in its output has a live citation — see [`01-agents.md`](01-agents.md#the-critic-agent). The PM pushes back on judgment calls, not on obviously unsourced claims; those never arrive. ## The four actions, same verbs as everywhere else | Action | What it does | |---|---| | **Accept** | Step → `accepted`. Its `Finding`/`Cluster`/`Requirement`/`Score` output becomes real input for the next step. Unlocks whatever depends on it. | | **Edit** | PM directly rewrites the human-readable summary or the underlying structured output (e.g. merges two clusters, tightens a metric) before accepting. The diff is the audit event. | | **Retry** (= Challenge, at step grain) | PM supplies a steering note ("exclude paywalled sources," "only EU respondents," "re-check that number"). Same agent, same step, re-runs with the note appended to its task. Step goes back to `running`. | | **Reject** | Step → `rejected`. PM then decides: proceed without this agent's contribution (flagged as a coverage gap on everything downstream) or abort the run. | This reuses the exact same four verbs as the coarser requirement lifecycle ([`05-requirement-lifecycle.md`](05-requirement-lifecycle.md)) — approve/reject/edit/challenge — just applied at the grain of one agent's output instead of one finished requirement. The lifecycle doc is what happens to a requirement *after* a run produces it and the PM gives the final accept; this doc is how that research got approved in the first place. ## Human-readable output, every time Every agent emits two things, not one: structured output for the data model, and a short `StepSummary` — plain language, always including: - what it looked at (scope, sources, filters applied) - what it found, as a short bulleted list, each bullet carrying its citation - how confident it is, and what's thin or missing - anything it flagged as out of scope (regulatory/pricing) and routed to the side bin This is what renders in the `awaiting_review` card. It is *not* a separate documentation step bolted on afterward — it's how the PM reviews anything at all. The Documentation Agent's job at stage 05 is to compile the already-accepted `StepSummary`s plus the final requirement into one coherent dossier, not to invent readability from scratch. ## The full chain ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph SA["01 Situation analysis — independent, PM launches each in any order"] direction LR A1[Baseline Agent] A2[Customer Feedback Agent] A3[Sales & Portfolio Agent] A4[Competitor Agent] A5[Market & Trend Agent] end SA -->|all accepted, or PM proceeds
with a flagged partial set| SC[02 Clustering / Structure & context] SC -->|accepted| RD[03 Requirements Drafting] RD -->|accepted — batch research
judged sound| PR[04 Prioritization / Scoring] PR -->|accepted| DOC[05 Documentation — dossier,
audit events, re-embed] DOC -->|PM final accept| FV["Final verdict:
each requirement → Draft
in the normal lifecycle"] ``` Note the last arrow: the "final verdict" of a run is not automatically `Tracked`. It hands each requirement into the normal [lifecycle](05-requirement-lifecycle.md) at `Draft`, where it can still be approved, edited, rejected, or challenged individually — a run can produce five candidate requirements that get decided on five different days by (possibly) five different reviewers. ## Worked example — "what features would we need to stay competitive in the US market?" 1. PM types the question into the run launcher, scoped to `{vehicle_line: G60, market: US}`. A new `PipelineRun` is created (`trigger: pm_query`). All five Situation Analysis steps appear as `awaiting_launch` cards — nothing has run yet. 2. PM clicks **Run** on the Competitor Agent first (their call — order isn't fixed). It finishes; card reads: *"Searched 14 competitor review/spec sources for US midsize sedans. 6 findings: 3 competitor_advantage, 2 market_trend, 1 unmet_need. 2 sources are paywalled — flagged Interpreted."* 3. PM clicks **Retry**: *"drop the paywalled ones, find a free equivalent or mark unverified."* Same agent re-runs. PM reviews again, clicks **Accept**. 4. PM clicks **Run** on Customer Feedback Agent (US-filtered), Sales & Portfolio Agent, and Market & Trend Agent in turn — three more independent click → review → accept cycles. Accepting one does not start the next; the PM clicks each one. 5. All five accepted → Clustering unlocks. PM runs it, **Edits** one cluster (two themes were really the same complaint), **Accepts**. 6. Requirements Drafting unlocks. PM runs it, reviews the drafted requirements as a batch, judges the research sound, **Accepts** — each draft now exists independently in the normal lifecycle. 7. Prioritization unlocks. PM reviews the score breakdown, nudges `business_signal` weight up for this program, re-runs, **Accepts**. 8. Documentation unlocks, compiles the dossier, writes every `AuditEvent` for the run, re-embeds it into the knowledge layer. PM gives the final accept. End state: a cited, ranked shortlist of candidate requirements sitting in the normal backlog at `Draft`, and an audit trail (see [`07-audit-trail.md`](07-audit-trail.md)) that shows exactly which agent ran when, what the PM retried and why, and what was accepted verbatim versus edited — not just a final answer with no visible work. ## Data model additions Two entities this doc introduces; full schema in [`04-data-model.md`](04-data-model.md#pipelinerun--step): `PipelineRun` (the scope + trigger of one execution) and `Step` (one agent's slot in it, with its state, its `StepSummary`, and who launched/accepted/retried/rejected it and why). ## UI shape A run view is a vertical stepper, one card per step, grouped by stage — not a single "run everything" button. A card's only possible actions are determined by its state: `awaiting_launch` shows **Run**; `awaiting_review` shows the `StepSummary` plus **Accept / Edit / Retry / Reject**; anything else is read-only history. This is deliberately closer to a CI pipeline with manual approval gates than to a chatbot — the PM is operating the system, not just chatting with it.

# 0002 — Gate every agent step, not just the drafted requirement and its score

> Date: 2026-10-10 · Status: accepted

## Context

The first pass at this architecture gated the PM in at two points: after a requirement was
drafted, and after it was scored. Everything upstream of drafting — four-plus research agents
reading feedback, option data, sales data, and the web — ran fully unattended and handed the PM a
single combined result to review at the end.

That's cheap to build but expensive to use: if the PM disagrees with one finding from the
Competitor Agent, there's no way to fix just that without re-running (or manually untangling) the
whole batch. It also means a PM can't steer research mid-flight ("focus on EU hot-climate
feedback") — only after the fact.

## Decision

Model a run as an ordered/partially-ordered sequence of `Step`s, one per agent invocation. A step
only starts when the PM explicitly clicks "Run" on it (not automatically, even once its
dependencies are satisfied), and its output — always rendered as a short human-readable summary,
never just raw structured data — only unlocks the next step once the PM clicks **Accept**. **Edit**,
**Retry** (with a steering note), and **Reject** are available at every step, not just at the end.

See [`../architecture/02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md`](../architecture/02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md).

## Consequences

- More PM clicks per run than a single end-of-pipeline review. Deliberate — the brief explicitly
  asks for the PM to be "firmly in control of every decision," not just the final one.
- Steering ("retry, but exclude X") becomes cheap and targeted instead of "reject everything, try
  again."
- The audit trail gains one entry per step action, not just one per finished requirement — more
  log volume, but it's what makes a run fully reconstructable after the fact (see
  [`../architecture/07-audit-trail.md`](../architecture/07-audit-trail.md)).
- Requires the orchestrator (LangGraph) to expose an `interrupt()` at every step boundary, not just
  two — informed the tech-stack choice, see
  [`../architecture/09-tech-stack.md`](../architecture/09-tech-stack.md).

Done — 15 files under `docs/`, all cross-linked, nothing committed yet (let me know if you want that).

**The key piece is `docs/architecture/02-orchestration-and-human-in-the-loop.md`** — it formalizes exactly what you described:

- A run is a sequence of `Step`s (one per agent). A step has five states: `queued → awaiting_launch → running → awaiting_review → accepted/rejected`.
- **`awaiting_launch` is a real, separate state** — accepting one step unlocks the next but does *not* auto-run it. The PM has to click "Run" on every single agent, which is literally "click to each agent step by step before it is run."
- Every agent output lands as a short human-readable `StepSummary` card (what it looked at, what it found, citations, confidence, what's thin) before the PM sees anything structured — that's the "put into human-readable format" requirement.
- Four actions at every step, reusing the same verbs as the rest of the system: **Accept** (unlocks the next agent), **Edit**, **Retry** (push back with a steering note, re-runs the *same* agent), **Reject**.
- A **Critic Agent** now sits between every agent and the PM, verifying citations and forcing a retry on unsupported claims *before* the step even reaches review — so the PM pushes back on judgment calls, not on obviously weak output.
- A full worked example walks the "what features do we need in the US market?" query through this exact click-by-click flow.

I also reconciled this with the rest of the design: `05-requirement-lifecycle.md` now explicitly says this step-chain is what happens *inside* a run, before a requirement even exists as `Draft`; the coarser approve/tracked/superseded lifecycle takes over afterward. Three ADRs in `docs/decisions/` record why (two-tier PDF ingestion, the step-gating shift, and folding in the Critic agent + Competitor/Trend split from the diagram you shared last).
